conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/5 - Medicine
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Formulated from one part powdered opium to nine parts alcohol and available in pre-mixed tinctures, it is an invaluable addition to one's home arsenal."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/5 - Medicine
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "...stomach trouble, female disorders, and insomnia to name but a few, it seems to have no end of uses."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/5 - Medicine
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up folk healing.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/5 - Medicine
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Many accomplished modern doctors and physicians have been born, raised, and trained in Ireland..."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/5 - Medicine
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "...and thus there is no shortage of such doctors there, Ireland is home to a parallel discipline known often as “folk healing”."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/5 - Medicine
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "That is, the tradition of treating ailments, common and uncommon, with hedge magic, from the tangible..."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/5 - Medicine
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "...(such as the application of herbal teas and tinctures)..."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/5 - Medicine
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "...to the intangible and somewhat more fantastical (often the creation or application of charms or rites)."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/5 - Medicine
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "While there is a belief that such ability is available to anyone, particular prowess is noted amongst a community..."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/5 - Medicine
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "...and often leads to one or two people being noted authorities on the practice within their communities."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/5 - Medicine
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up quinine.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/5 - Medicine
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Extracted in India from the bark of the Cinchona tree, quinine was used in 17th-century South America as a treatment for malaria and fevers. Through British trade networks, quinine became commonplace in Irish medicine as a general fever remedy. It can be purchased from chemists and apothecaries in pre-mixed tinctures and tonics, as well as in pill and powder form."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/5 - Medicine
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Quinine sulphate powder is often sold in small quantities without the need for a prescription. Due to its dreadfully bitter taste, it is recommended to mix it with water, sugar, or spirits for easier consumption."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/5 - Medicine
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "In high doses, its side effects may include dizziness, numbness, and dulling of the senses. In severe cases, it can cause nausea, confusion, and temporary blindness. Yet quinine remains the preferred option for many, as its side effects are less harmful and addictive than most opioid alternatives."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/5 - Medicine
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Although its distribution has been regulated since 1868, along with opiates and arsenic-based substances, high doses of quinine can still be obtained in Ireland from local chemist shops upon presentation of a physician’s order."

speaker: Detective Ward

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/13 - Geography
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up the Ulster region.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/13 - Geography
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up the Munster region.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/13 - Geography
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The westernmost province of Ireland, once a collection of kingdoms, and site of and witness to two of the most terrible battles in Irish history...

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/13 - Geography
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The northernmost province of the four provinces of Ireland, and once the heart of the Gaelic world, today Ulster holds the greatest population...

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/13 - Geography
speaker: Mister Ward
en: ...while interceded with significant periods of peace, Connacht has a history of warfare."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/13 - Geography
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Party to the Irish rebellion against the Crown, aided by French forces, and backdrop to the Cromwellian conquest...

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/13 - Geography
speaker: Mister Ward
en: ...Connacht is a much contested stronghold of Irish culture."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/13 - Geography
speaker: Mister Ward
en: ...of Protestants and Loyalists to the Crown after the country of Ireland was adopted into the United Kingdom in 1801."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/13 - Geography
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Ulster was previously a region of importance to Irish sovereignty, it being the seat of power from where one of five “King-above-kings” would rule."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/13 - Geography
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Belfast is the largest city in the region, on the border of counties Antrim and Down, and is a significant centre of populace in Ireland as a whole."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/13 - Geography
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The southernmost province of Ireland's four provinces, Munster was where the most of Saint Patrick's work bringing Christianity to Ireland took place."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/13 - Geography
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "With this, and several cities (Cork and Waterford among them) founded by Viking settlers, Munster has long had a tradition of transformative visitations."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/13 - Geography
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Not least of these being the colonisation of the region by the English in the 16th century, a most significant venture by the Crown."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/13 - Geography
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up the Leinster region.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/13 - Geography
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The easternmost province of Ireland, Leinster was home to many Celtic Tribes, most notably the Laighin to which the province owes its name."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/13 - Geography
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Vikings made their arrival to Ireland and by the mid-9th Century had transitioned from raiding to settling, with Dublin being their most significant settlement - serving as a major trade center and later becoming a Norse-Gaelic kingdom. This would not last, as the Vikings were later driven out by native Irish rulers."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/13 - Geography
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Leinster has seen a long history of territorial battles, ranging from the arrival of Anglo-Normans in the late 12th Century - leading to the broader invasion of English forces - to a Gaelic resurgence in the middle ages, followed by the Tudors solidifying English control over Ireland by the 16th Century."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/13 - Geography
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "More recently, the Cromwellian Conquest landed in Dublin with twelve thousand troops and travelled north to begin an assault that would later be known as the Siege of Drogheda, or the ‘Drogheda Massacre’. Its surviving rebels being transported to the overcrowded gaol of Dundalk, where they were left to starve and die. This would only be the beginning of Oliver’s devastating campaign on Irish soil."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/13 - Geography
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "This region housed a collection of small Kingdoms and dynasties, with the Hill of Tara in particular, located in Mide (later named ‘Meath’), holding significant spiritual and political power as the seat of the High Kings of Ireland."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/13 - Geography
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up the Blake Manor.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/13 - Geography
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Construction on Blake Castle began in 1652, on land awarded to the veteran soldier Edward Blake."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/13 - Geography
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "It was a matter of no small undertaking or finance, and the work continued over generations."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/13 - Geography
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "It is said that the manor was built on ground the local residents considered to have once been sacred, but records of this do not exist."

speaker: Detective Ward

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up the Tsunami of 1755.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up the Great Freeze.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: The first of Ireland's three famines. Crop and herd damage from the Great Freeze resulted in massive shortages in milk and food.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: In the winter of 1739 a violent storm hit Ireland. The resultant drop in temperature was so drastic, that liquids froze indoors.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Massive earthquakes in Portugal sent a tsunami north that hit the southern and western parts of Ireland."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up the Great Famine.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "It's less than fifty years since the Great Hunger that lasted from '45 to '52."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: There are no official records of how cold it got but some measurements taken by enthusiasts claim it dropped as low as minus twenty degrees.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: Records suggest that as high as twenty percent of the then population died.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: It was a higher proportion of lives lost than from the Great Famine nearly a century later.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "It seems to have reached as far up as Connemara, where this manor is built."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Untold thousands died here from the tsunami. The earthquake itself claimed the lives of over one-hundred-thousand Portuguese."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: Anyone surviving something like that can't but have deep scars. My own parents refused to talk of it and grew dark when it was mentioned.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "A blight wiped out the potato crops. Most of the population relied on that to survive, as the English rule exported every other resource from the country - peas, beans, rabbits, fish, honey, and more."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Ontop of this, the English Corn Laws blocked the import of any grain, despite the obvious need for relief."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The full loss of life from this period is yet unknown, but deaths are estimated to be around one million, with another million fleeing the country on coffin ships bound for America, Canada, Australia, and more."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: It is unknown how long it will take the country to recover.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up the symbol on Miss Barbosa's brooch >

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: There's a book here on family crests. This might have what I need.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up standing stones.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Standing stones, or menhir, are large, deliberately placed stones found around the world, but especially in Ireland."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "There is no consensus on the purpose of standing stones; there are no records detailing it, nor any surviving traditions that can be reliably traced."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "However, there are several theories as to their purpose. Those most commonly held would posit that they marked the boundaries of territories."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Or, that they had ritual significance to old druidic religion."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Some menhir - cloch fhada in the Irish tongue - are found to be inscribed with a long-forgotten, and therefore indiscernible, language."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up the O'Connor family.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: While there are several branches of the O’Connor family, a notable lineage in the Connacht Region seems to have been almost destroyed in the late 1700s.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: A devoutly Catholic line, there are indications that their covertly held belief was betrayed to the Crown, resulting in their execution.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: Those remaining family members were scattered to the winds, and if any remain, their current whereabouts are unknown.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up Ogham carvings.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up Keening.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Keening, or lamenting over the dead, is an ancient custom practised in Ireland, with origins tracing back to Eastern nations."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The Irish word for keening, "cine," closely resembles the Hebrew "cina," both meaning lamentation or weeping with clapping of hands."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Traditionally, Irish bards led the funeral songs, that addressed the deceased’s genealogy, rank, possessions, virtues and vices. But over time, hired mourners - often women - took over."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Till about the middle of the last century, the custom was very generally adhered to in Ireland, as well in families of the highest condition, as among those of the lower orders."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Of late years, the custom has fallen greatly into disuse, and is now of rare occurrence, except in some very few old families, and among the peasantry, and has become more of a wordless, mournful cry"

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up the Magdalene Asylum.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Magdalene Asylum originates from convent-run institutions for “fallen” women, which began in 13th-century Italy."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Mary Magdalene was an ideal symbol for the institutions as she is often associated with repentance, devotion, and the power of grace.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "A network of convents and institutions expanded across Italy and Catholic Europe, providing secluded spaces for women seeking penance, particularly former prostitutes."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "In 18th-century England, philanthropists founded institutions like the Magdalene Hospital, adapting Catholic models to Protestant contexts for the care and rehabilitation of vulnerable women."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/2 - Irish History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "This was later brought to Ireland by a Protestant philanthropist, Lady Arabella Denny, who founded Ireland’s first Magdalene Asylum in 1767."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/7 - Psychology and Philosophy

en: Perhaps I could try this technique and use the knowledge of the shared dreams as my anchor? I could use Miss Deane's journal to represent that.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/7 - Psychology and Philosophy
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Dreams are part of the sleep experience and act as a way to process one's experiences of that day."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/7 - Psychology and Philosophy

en: "They are often abstract and sometimes surreal and range from pleasant to frightening."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/7 - Psychology and Philosophy
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Since dreams are mercurial and often soon forgotten after sleep, many people turn to lucid dreaming to better control and recall."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Instrumental in the execution of King Charles I and the brief period in which England became a commonwealth in the 1600s..."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Even in his homeland, Cromwell was a controversial figure, infamous for his ban on the celebration of Christmas among many such joyful activities..."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "...as they were thought to distract from the worship of God."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "While widely disliked in England, his legacy in Ireland is significantly darker and more bloody."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "In what became known as the "Cromwellian Conquest", Cromwell lead what amounted to a massacre across Ireland in the form of a conquest."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "He spared no quarter, going so far as to order the deaths of even those who had sheltered in churches, such as in the Siege of Drogheda."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up the Brazilian Revolution.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: Portugal claimed control over Brazil in 1500 and ruled it as a colony for three centuries.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: When the Portuguese royal family fled there in 1807

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The Paraguay War, also known as The War of the Triple Alliance, lasted from 1864 to 1870."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up the Paraguay War.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The results of the Uruguay War were the cause of the conflict between Paraguay and Brazil, which led to the Paraguay War."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Paraguay was defeated in 1869 but resorted to guerrilla warfare for another 14 months, resulting in significant destruction and loss of life among both military and civilians."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "In March 1870, the war concluded with the death of Paraguayan president Francisco Solano López, leaving the country open to occupation by foreign troops."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The Brazilian Naval Revolts were led by admirals Custódio José de Melo and Saldanha da Gama against President Floriano Peixoto's rule."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up the Brazilian Revolt.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The tensions started in November 1891, and resulted in a 7 month long revolt that ended on March 1894."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "With many naval ships in the hands of rebels, the government resorted to forming an improved fleet called the "paper fleet" to respond."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "This turmoil resulted in bloody conflicts across Brazil."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up Mardi Gras.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Mardi Gras, meaning "Fat Tuesday," is celebrated on the day before Ash Wednesday, marking the beginning of Lent."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "It has its origins in French Catholic tradition and was brought to North America by the Le Moyne brothers in the late 17th century."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The tradition of having parades during the celebration in New Orleans started in 1853 and has been continued ever since."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Masks and costumes are often donned by the participants of the festival in celebratory colours to invoke the vibrancy of life."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up Carnival.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Carnival is a lively celebration that emphasizes the joy of life before the Christian season of Lent."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Unlike Mardi Gras, Carnival is not limited to just one day, spanning from January to March, with festivities culminating on the Tuesday before Ash Wednesday."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The celebrations are marked by vibrant floats, elaborate costumes, and massive parades with the rhythm, participation, and style of costumes differing from region to region."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Quilombos are settlements established by escaped Afro-Brazilian slaves. Many of the settlement’s residents live in poverty"

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up the Quilombolas.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "These communities originated during the 16th century in Brazil, when Afro-Brazilian slaves fled brutal conditions on sugar plantations in Brazil."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "It is said that Aqualtune, an Angolan princess and general who was enslaved during a Congolese war, escaped with some of her soldiers and founded Palamares, which is one of the largest quilombos in Brazil."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Capitães-do-mato, which translates to Captain of the Forest, were free men, usually of limited financial means, tasked with hunting and recapturing escaped slaves in Brazil."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up the Captain of the Forest.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Their main job was to return fugitives to their masters and to destroy quilombo settlements, receiving monetary rewards in return."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Most capitães-do-mato were freed slaves themselves, which put them above slaves but still low in social prestige and made them resented by captives."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/3 - World History
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Despite their authority, they were generally looked down upon and remained close to the social position of those they pursued."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up Gnosticism.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Mister Ward
en: Copies of the bible sit here with core texts of other faiths. It's interesting to see this so openly displayed - to some this would be blasphemous.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Mister Ward
en: Is there anything I want to look up?

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up Celtic crosses.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The Celtic cross is distinguished from the Latin cross by the circle, or "nimbus", around its intersection."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Its formation is attributed to Ireland, France, and Great Britain, and it gained prominence in medieval art."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Its designation as the "Celtic Cross" is relatively recent, perhaps reflective of its historic use among Irish missionaries."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up Celtic religious symbols.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "There are a number of designs synonymous with Celtic culture and spirituality. I list here a few."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The Triskelion: Three spirals joined together at their outermost points and the centre of the design."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Thought to represent the physical world, the spirit world, and the afterlife - or alternatively, birth, life, and death."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The Triquetra: An ancient symbol of a tri-pointed endless knot, now understood to represent the Holy Trinity."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The Dara Knot: A complicated square knot without end. Associated with Saint Patrick, patron saint of Ireland..."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "...the Dara Knot is a symbol of unity and peace."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up the resurrectix.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Where a crucifix depicts Jesus Christ in His crucifixion, and so speaks to His sacrifice and the forgiveness bestowed upon Humanity for it..."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "A resurrectix is the crucifix's counterpart; the cross upon which Jesus was crucified, with no depiction of the Lord upon it."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The resurrectix, then, is an empty cross - the Lord having departed it - and in this, it signifies hope, eternal life, and triumph over death."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up Samhain.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Samhain, approximately pronounced Sah-wen, is a Gaelic festival traditionally occurring on the first of November..."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "...towards the end of the harvest season and at the beginning of winter."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Believed to be born of pagan tradition, the festival represents a time in the year where the boundaries between the mundane world and the Otherworld would weaken..."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "...and as such many traditions associated with the festival are thought to be protective, to ward away the spirits that would otherwise broach the boundary and cause the living harm."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "During this time, spirits were to be appeased with offerings of food and drink, so that they would leave the living in peace throughout the rest of the year."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up draoi.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The native Irish word for a traditional practitioner of magic and ritual, a draoi (pronounced dree)..."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "...might be considered equivalent to a wizard or sorcerer, perhaps one with religious prestige within their community."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "However, their nature remains the source of speculation, as they remain a feature of antiquity."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "While the author of this book has encountered rumour of their continued existence, I was unable to verify their truthfulness."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up pagan sacred sites.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "While much of the knowledge of sites of religious significance to the pre-Christian pagans has been lost, there are several that have been identified across the country."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Stone circles apparently constructed for ritual purpose abound, and burial sites such as those found in Newgrange suggest a reverence for the movements of the heavens."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Some old sacred sites seem to have been co-opted into modern tradition..."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "...as there remains a tradition of lone oak trees being best left undisturbed so as not to upset Otherworldly spirits."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "A superstition which does not hold the same prevalence and longevity in other parts of the United Kingdom."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Nothing right now...

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up The Ten Commandments.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Mister Ward
en: A list of tenets central to Judaism and Christianity.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/8 - Religion
speaker: Mister Ward
en: I am the Lord thy God, thou shalt have no other gods before me; Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain; Thous shalt keep the Lord's Day holy; Honor thy father and thy mother; Thou shalt not kill; Thou shalt not commit adultery; Thou shalt not steal; Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour; Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife; Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's good.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/12 - World Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: Books on the various mythologies across the world, though the focus is heavily on the classics and Egypt.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/12 - World Mythology
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Nothing right now...

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/12 - World Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: Is there anything I want to look up?

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/12 - World Mythology
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up Vampires.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/12 - World Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Undead humans who survive by draining the blood of the living."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/12 - World Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "A common supernatural element in most European cultures."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/12 - World Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Examples include the Albanian shtriga, Greek vrykolakas, Romanian strigoi, and Irish abhartach."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/12 - World Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The Irish abhartach was called a dwarf for its child-like proportions."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/12 - World Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Despite its anger and blood thirst, its subjects were drawn to it, as if under a spell."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/12 - World Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "They are nigh-impossible to kill, being vulnerable only to wood from the yew tree."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/12 - World Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Even then, once killed it needs to be buried upside down and weighed down with a stone of such a size that it would take at least five good men to move it."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/12 - World Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "For these reasons is said that once a land is plagued by an abhartach they are never to truly be free from it; that it will return to feed on generation after generation."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: A section on Irish folklore and ghost tales.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Nothing right now...

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: Is there anything I want to look up?

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up turnip heads.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Towards the end of October and with the approach of Halloween, it is not uncommon to see carved lanterns adorning doorsteps and windowsills."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "In Ireland and Scotland both, there is a long-held tradition of carving a face into turnips, and putting a lit candle inside them."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The tradition is thought to stem from the Irish folktale of "Stingy Jack", a spirit barred from both heaven and hell and forced to walk the earth eternally."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Whether this is true or not, these carved turnips are thought to serve a practical purpose."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "It is thought that on Halloween night, the veil between life and death is thin, and spirits walk to earth - many with ill intent."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "These turnips are carved into grotesque faces and lit as lanterns to ward off any spirits that would do the living harm."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up the bean sídhe.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The bean-sídhe, often Anglicized as "banshee", is a faerie woman who portends death."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "She is often said to appear in a grey cloak and a green dress, with eyes red from crying."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "To hear her keening means there will soon be a death in one's life - typically on that same night - and frequently of a loved one or family member."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up the Aoi Sí.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Aoi Sí means 'People of the mound' and covers all entities that come from the Other World."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "This covers the Fae Folk, the old gods, and any of the other range of creatures from that place."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "For some, ghosts are also included as the Other World encompasses the Irish land of the dead."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The fae themselves range in power from god-like, legendary figures, to the types more thought to commonly occur and roam the landscape..."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "...often looking to cause mischief or harm, such that to invite their attention is considered bad luck."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The nature of the fae, as with humanity’s, varies by instance, but an estimate can be made by the type of the fae in question."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Some look to cause harm; some are portents of ill-tidings, but do not seem to cause it themselves..."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "...and some (though these cases are occasional) may even be beneficial to those encountering them."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Regardless, it is widely held that the safest course of interaction with the fae is not to interact with them at all."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up the Fear Gorta.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The fear gorta, (literally a “man of hunger”) is a type of apparition that is linked to the Great Famine."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "(Though there are alternate accounts that consider it an omen of further famines to come)."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Taking the form of a starving person, the fear gorta is a spirit of hunger, who will follow people to ask for food."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Should it catch its prey, it will not hesitate to consume them to satisfy its hunger."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up the washer woman.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The washer woman, or the bean nigh, is an instance of the Other Folk providing unwelcome news without exhibiting aggression or violence."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The apparition is said to appear before battle, where she will be seen washing the bloody armour of those to die, as if they are already dead."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Is it said she appears at battlegrounds as she feeds off of grief. Perhaps, this is why she shows visions of those to die?"

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Always unsuccessful in quenching its hunger, it then seeks out a new victim..."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up Suibne.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The Madness of Suibne tells the story of Suibne mac Colmain, a king of the Dál nAraidi (a region in the Northeast or Ireland), who tried to expel Bishop Ronan from church activities on his land."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Suibne eventually attempts to murder the Bishop and succeeds in killing the Bishop’s psalmists with a spear."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "In response, Bishop Ronan cursed Suibne that he would wander the land like a bird, and second, that he would eventually die by the spear, just as he had killed the monk"

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The tale describes how Suibne wandered the world as a madman, moving from tree to tree until he eventually dies in the very way the curse was detailed."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Throughout his mad wanderings, Suibne occasionally stops at each location to recite a poem. Some say that anyone who sees the bird or hears the poems will themselves be driven to madness."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/10 - Irish Folklore
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "They are believed by the Irish to live in this world, largely apart from humanity and the mundane... but not entirely."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/14 - Archaeology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: Is there anything I want to look up?

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/14 - Archaeology
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up canopic jars.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/14 - Archaeology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Canopic jars were used in Ancient Egyptian burials to hold the significant major organs of the mummified person, typically decorated with images of gods."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/14 - Archaeology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The belief was that a person would need the soul of their viscera in the afterlife, and the canopic jars were intended to store them until such a time."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/14 - Archaeology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "There would be four canopic jars per mummified person; one to contain the stomach, one to contain the liver, one to contain the lungs, and one to contain the intestines."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/14 - Archaeology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "In the later period, the once-plain jars would be topped with the figure of a god, one of the four sons of Horus, each also associated with a companion goddess and a cardinal direction."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/14 - Archaeology
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up Vase of Nectanebo.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: A mix of guides on spiritual matters, guides for making contact, and a record of, supposedly real, encounters with the afterlife.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Nothing right now...

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: Is there anything I want to look up?

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up the Second Sight.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The Second Sight is a skill possessed by some that allows them to know of the future, or events far from them they should rightly have no knowledge of."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up tarot cards.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Originally a type of card deck used for various Italian games, the tarot card was later adopted by the French for use in divination, or "cartomancy"."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "This being a publication unconcerned with such mundane issues as simple card games, we will disregard the traditional use for its magical cousin."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "A tarot deck consists of seventy-eight cards and two Arcana, the twenty-one Major Arcana being "face cards", and the Minor Arcana being suits."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The Minor Arcana is divided into four suits (Wands, Swords, Cups, and Coins) and consists of cards of numbers one to ten, and four court cards."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Each Major Arcana has specific meaning, as does every suit and its cards therein; and every card has another meaning again if drawn in the reversed position."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Tarot cards are to be drawn one by one in formation, and read with consideration of their individual meaning and their position in the draw."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "They are typically consulted in matters of love and fortune, but can be asked a great many things - and, in general, are favoured for their versatility."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up séances.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "A séance is a ritual used to speak with the dead, typically hosted by a spirit medium, but attended and aided by a number of guests."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "A spirit is called upon by the medium, and asked questions. It will answer them through physical means, such as moving a glass on a board..."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "...through audible means, such as knocking, or, if one is so lucky, by the possession of one of those at the table."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "In this case, the spirit is frequently able to articulate itself better, although some may find it to be a distressing sight."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Séances are typically used by still-living loved ones to speak to those they have lost, or to divine secrets known only to the dead."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "In Scotland, it is thought to run in families, especially those in the highlands, and while the information gleaned through this mystic sense can be useful, it can also be harrowing."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "It can also refer to the ability to see the dead."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Sight alone does not mean understanding, nor can dark visions of the future necessarily be averted, though those with the Sight are often compelled to try."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up ghosts.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "There is much debate over the true nature of ghosts - even their existence in the first place! - but there are two major prevailing theories."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The first is that a ghost is a remnant of a person - a soul that, for whatever reason, has not passed on."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "This sort of ghost is typically attributed to the need for some desire of the soul - or the person it was - to be sated, be it revenge, ambition, or love."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "In a similar vein, they frequently cling to some object or place of importance, unable to complete whatever business holds them there in their new state."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "A secondary, less discussed - but widely credited - theory of the cause of apparitions is the manifestation of emotion or trauma."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "In this theory, it is thought that human beings are capable of imparting such emotion that it forever affects the location that witnesses it."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "In these cases, it is not the spirit itself that haunts a place, but the event - typically a harrowing death - imprinting itself upon a space."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "These theories are not exclusive, and could very well exist alongside each other. Such is the prevalence of spirits that it seems unlikely both are not true."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up the Society for Psychical Research.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: Established in London, 1882, the Society for Psychical Research endeavours to investigate psychical matters and occurrences...

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Without prejudice or prepossession of any kind, and in the same spirit of exact and unimpassioned enquiry."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: It publishes a regular journal and intermittent studies as to the society's findings, and its membership includes both "believers" and sceptics.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "To the layperson, not much is known about the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn (henceforth "the Golden Dawn")."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "It is a secret magical society, founded in England, although it is rumoured to have further branches."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Reportedly, the Golden Dawn's focus is on divine magic and spiritual development, though the specifics of this are unknown."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Despite the Golden Dawn's enigmatic nature, its members may be recognised by its symbol..."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "A Latin cross with a rose in its centre, and a pentagram and several alchemical symbols on each arm."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up mystics.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "There exist among us certain people predisposed to sensing and invoking the ebb and flow of the spiritual world and its denizens."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "These people, often called mystics – as indeed I will refer to them here! – possess a unique capability."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "They are able to sense the supernatural and Otherworldly and in doing so provide means of communication with it, often using themselves as the go-between."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "This is most commonly achieved by invoking a trance or otherwise altered state through spell, prayer, or ritual..."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "...and inviting either a spirit, a higher power, or a denizen from another world to speak through them."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: … though uncommonly encountered, an ancient binding ritual forged the creation of a particular rune used for the purpose of that binding and that alone.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: A spiral with four intersecting lines (one at the top, three at the bottom) is thought to represent a gateway to the Otherworld...

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: ...the bound gods’ blood, and the three human clans who bound them, this symbol being used by the Milesians to seal off the Otherworld.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up occult orders.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: There are any number of occult orders, some better known than others.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: It is truly impossible to know quite how many there are, as many hold a tradition of secrecy.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: Those at least deigning to let their existence be known include the Freemasons and the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn…

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: But truth be told there may be many more than are known, either through secrecy or relative informality.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: Certainly, initially informal groups that may gather for rites or rituals such as séances have a tendency to take such form, once the anteed are sufficiently fervent.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up ritual markings.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up fetters.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "‘Soul trapping’, or the unwillful binding of souls to inanimate objects, is a phenomenon that has been recorded throughout history and across the known world. One such instance occurred during an expedition to Egypt conducted by Lord Thomas Blake of Doon. A number of what locals termed ‘soul jars’ were unearthed near a tomb and were brought to Dublin by Lord Blake for further examination."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "In a drunken stupor, Lord Blake’s young apprentice Harry Arnold cracked his skull on an ancient tablet in Blake’s office and died almost immediately."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Lord Blake, upon hearing the lad’s anguished screams, ran to the office to find his apprentice’s lifeless corpse bleeding out on the bench. The screams, he soon realised, were coming from one of the soul jars and, to quell the wailing, Blake ordered that the jars be destroyed."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Elsewhere in the world, there are stories of the souls of the recently departed being tied to objects of strong emotional significance. These objects, known as ‘fetters’, can take any form; fetters as small as a needle and as large as a carriage have been documented across the world."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/9 - Spiritualism and Ghost Sightings
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Some spiritualists theorise that even entire buildings or areas of land can, under specific circumstances, become fetters, though no evidence of such a phenomenon has been found thus far. Others disagree with this assertion; they argue that the force of emotion needed to tie souls to something as large as a building or as intangible as an area of land would be, frankly, inhuman."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/- Engineering
speaker: Mister Ward
en: Everything from steam engine schematics to how telephones works can be found here.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/- Engineering
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Nothing right now...

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/- Engineering
speaker: Mister Ward
en: Is there anything I want to look up?

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/- Travel
speaker: Mister Ward
en: Information on the world's countries are kept here with information on how to travel to them - sailing information, navigation maps, and even treatises on the theory of human flight.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/- Travel
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Nothing right now...

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/- Travel
speaker: Mister Ward
en: Is there anything I want to look up?

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/- Travel
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up Mardi Gras.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/- Travel
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Mardi Gras, meaning "Fat Tuesday," is celebrated on the day before Ash Wednesday, marking the beginning of Lent."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/- Travel
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "It has its origins in French Catholic tradition and was brought to North America by the Le Moyne brothers in the late 17th century."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/- Travel
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The tradition of having parades during the celebration in New Orleans started in 1853 and has been continued ever since."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/- Travel
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Masks and costumes are often donned by the participants of the festival in celebratory colours to invoke the vibrancy of life."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/- Travel
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up Brazilian Carnival.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/- Travel
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Carnival is a lively celebration that emphasizes the joy of life before the Christian season of Lent."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/- Travel
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Unlike Mardi Gras, Carnival is not limited to just one day, spanning from January to March, with festivities culminating on the Tuesday before Ash Wednesday."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/- Travel
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The celebrations are marked by vibrant floats, elaborate costumes, and massive parades with the rhythm, participation, and style of costumes differing from region to region."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: A collection of books on the four cycles of Irish mythology are here, alongside writings on supernatural sites and entities.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Nothing right now...

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: Is there anything I want to look up?

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up the Veil.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The Veil is the barrier between the living and the dead; the mundane world and the spirit world."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "There are times and places when the Veil thins, and interaction between the two worlds becomes easier... for better or for worse."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The Veil may be thin in places that have seen great tragedy, or in places of magical significance."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "As for time, it is known that the Veil is thinnest on All Hallow's Eve, and this is when spirits of many kinds may walk the earth..."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "...and be seen even by those who usually would not encounter such things. It is also when communication through the Veil is easiest."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "As such, traditionally any attempts to contact the dead are made in this period of the year, as they are known to be most successful at this time."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up Milesians.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "That's when the gods disappeared underground and mankind settled this land."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The tribe of mankind. A word for the ancient Irish, I suppose, from which many of us are descended."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Led here thousands of years ago by three chieftain-brothers - Éber Finn, Amergin, and Eremon - who were said to be powerful sorcerers."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "They clashed with the old gods, the Tuatha Dé Danann, and reached a truce after much fighting."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "They agreed to split the land in half between them. But the Milesians tricked the old gods and picked "the top half"."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Irish mythology has its share of giants, but none so noteworthy as Fionn mac Cumhaill."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up Giants.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "There are some who believe him to be the demigod descendant of MacCuill, the last king of the Tuatha Dé Danann."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The Tuatha Dé Danann, or people of Danu, are the old gods of Ireland, with Danu being a sort of earth mother type entity representing the land itself."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up Tuatha Dé Danann.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "A race of beings, each twice the height of a man, with unnatural abilities. Like the gods of many classical mythologies, each one had areas of expertise though there was much overlapping and infighting as a result."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up The Fate of the Gods.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Detective Ward
en: Look up Tír na nÓg.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: I can't find anything. It looks like any books on it have been taken away. I should ask around for more information.

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The bearer of the Thumb of Knowledge and leader of the legendary band of warriors, the Fianna, Fionn has many tales attributed to him:"

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The formation of the Giant's Causeway, the creation of the Isle of Man and Lough Neagh, and the battling of many mythological foes."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "They lived across Ireland for countless centuries and battled with various Otherworldly foes."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Eventually, after too much loss, a truce was reached and it was agreed that the land would be split evenly between both parties."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The Battle of Tailtiu was a fierce battle fought between the Tuatha Dé Danann and the Milesians that lasted many days and saw both sides using underhanded tactics."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "But the Milesians tricked the gods for when it was their time to pick, they picked "the top half"."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "The gods, true to their word accepted the deal and moved underground to Tír na nÓg, part of the Otherworld, to live with the fae."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "To show their goodwill, the gods let the Milesians choose their half first."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "There is a book here with some of the Tuatha Dé Danann listed in it. It might be worth a look."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/11 - Irish Mythology
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Throughout his mad wanderings, Suibne occasionally stops at each location to recite a poem. The vivid depictions of the countryside, nature, and his plight are key elements that shape the text."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/WilhelminaBlake
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Wilhelmina August Blake was born in 1788 to Thomas Blake, the sixth Marquess of Doon. She disappeared without a trace on the night of October 29th 1828."

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/WilhelminaBlake
speaker: Mister Ward

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/Mary Blake

conversation: Ground floor/Library/comments from Ward/Bookshelves/Mary Blake

speaker: Mister O'Meara
en: Oh, I nearly died.

conversation: Ground floor/Bar/Eavesdrop Cathal and D'Arcy
speaker: Missus D'Arcy
en: Go on...

conversation: Ground floor/Bar/Eavesdrop Cathal and D'Arcy
speaker: Mister O'Meara
en: Hah. A horse riding accident, just over a year ago. You know how it is, the horse spooks, and there's only so much you can do.

conversation: Ground floor/Bar/Eavesdrop Cathal and D'Arcy
speaker: Mister O'Meara
en: I don't remember much of what happened after I fell. Not what was around me, anyway. Just the most... revolting pain in my side and my leg.

conversation: Ground floor/Bar/Eavesdrop Cathal and D'Arcy
speaker: Mister O'Meara
en: And the idea that I was going to die. I can't say it seemed clear, because nothing was, but it did seem very certain.

conversation: Ground floor/Bar/Eavesdrop Cathal and D'Arcy
speaker: Mister O'Meara
en: And then I saw... I still don't know how to describe what it looked like. But behind all that was happening around me, I saw it - a thing that I instinctively knew was an angel.

conversation: Ground floor/Bar/Eavesdrop Cathal and D'Arcy
speaker: Mister O'Meara
en: My companions got me to a doctor - all the while I would see glimpses of it watching. I was babbling the entire time, I am told.

conversation: Ground floor/Bar/Eavesdrop Cathal and D'Arcy
speaker: Mister O'Meara
en: I... It is around me, still. I get glimpses of it now and again. At some cost I can see it more clearly for a moment. I think it watches me, us - this séance.

conversation: Ground floor/Bar/Eavesdrop Cathal and D'Arcy
speaker: Missus D'Arcy
en: And you speak with it?

conversation: Ground floor/Bar/Eavesdrop Cathal and D'Arcy
speaker: Mister O'Meara
en: I wonder if it has some purpose for me, but it never stays around long enough to get an answer. To look upon it alone is just unmatched...

conversation: Ground floor/Bar/Eavesdrop Cathal and D'Arcy
speaker: Mister O'Meara
en: I speak to it. Sometimes. It does not reply.  If I am ill, or in danger, or on the brink of consciousness, I can make it out. See its shape, exchange a few words...

conversation: Ground floor/Bar/Eavesdrop Cathal and D'Arcy
speaker: Mister O'Meara
en: But the fact of the matter is, until the rituals work, those moments are all I get.

conversation: Ground floor/Bar/Eavesdrop Cathal and D'Arcy
speaker: Mister O'Meara
en: It stayed with me until the turn of midnight, and by then they thought I would live after all.

conversation: Ground floor/Bar/Eavesdrop Cathal and D'Arcy
speaker: Missus D'Arcy
en: And that was the end of it?

conversation: Ground floor/Bar/Eavesdrop Cathal and D'Arcy
speaker: Missus D'Arcy
en: Has the year last seen you ill, in danger, or on the brink of consciousness much?
