conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Blake on blake manor
speaker: Marquess Blake
en: That's perhaps a better question for Miss Mantovani...

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Blake on blake manor
speaker: Mister Coventry
en: The Blake family once owned all the land in this area. 20,000 acres was assigned to them, or 35 square miles. Even now all you can see from this manor still belongs to the family.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Blake on blake manor
speaker: Mister Coventry
en: Of course, much of this land isn't particularly farmable, so what was missing in quality was made up in quantity.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. I am Doctor Ruairí Callaghan, and I'm pleased to see you all here.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: I'd like to give my thanks, first of all - to you good people for attending this talk of mine, and to the Marquess for inviting me to speak.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: I’m going to talk to you today about the mythology of Ireland - the generations of mythical figures that were said to walk this land before us…

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: …and the story of our forefathers, as legend tells it, and how they secured our place here on this small part of the planet that we call home.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Detective Ward
en: [ STAY AND LISTEN ]

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Detective Ward
en: [ LEAVE ]

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Mister Ward
en: If you would excuse me...

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: It will help you to understand that there are four cycles in Irish mythology. First, there is the Mythological Cycle.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: It concerns the most ancient reaches of our mythology, a time when a godlike race, the Tuatha De Danann...

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: Secondly, there is the Ulster Cycle, which took place around the birth of Christ.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: It mostly concerns the warfare of the regional kingdoms that made up what we now know as Ireland.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: The third cycle is the Fenian Cycle, which focuses less on gods and their ilk, or even royalty. It concerns itself with exploits of hunters and bards, especially the Fianna, led by the hero Fionn Mac Cumhaill.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: And finally, there is the fourth cycle - the Cycle of Kings. This cycle, as you may guess, tells the story of the kings of Ireland, often with a moral to their story about the qualities that are desirable – or undesirable – in a king.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: The fourth cycle is also that in which we find the story of the Milesians, our forefathers, those who would win a battle against the Tuatha Dé Danann.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: ...shared this land with the Aos Sí or the Fair Folk - on which my aunt has already spoken to you.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: …Even after the first cycle, where they are seen most often, the Tuatha Dé Danann occur in many tales throughout Irish mythology.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: …Which brings me to the Milesians.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: Thank you all so much for listening.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: They are not gods in the Christian sense – they do not have the same level of power, nor are they all-knowing.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: Rather, they are more akin to the gods found in Ancient Greece or Rome.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: They are understood to have dominion over certain aspects of life, yes.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: But they were also understood to exist in a form possible for mortals to encounter, and bound by degrees of the practical nature this implies.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: Their plans, as we find in these myths, can be waylaid or circumvented by wily heroes.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: Ireland herself is often seen incarnate in the Fourth Cycle as a bride to a worthy king, demonstrating how the figures found in the narrative and the ideas they embody can become enmeshed...

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: ...And how, immortal as the ideas and domains of the Tuatha Dé Danann are, their kind can still be harmed, defeated, or even killed by adversaries - whomsoever those may be.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: The immortal nature of their domain, too, means that while we now live in a more enlightened age, we must not be so quick to dismiss these stories as entirely fantasy.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: Where the heart of a story has bearing in reality, you will often find some surrounding elements do, too.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: It may be that some of the stories we find in the mythological cycles are the accounts of actual happenings, made legendary through their retelling.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: This holds particular weight when one considers that we all know an element of the stories' supernatural aspects - being here as magicians ourselves, to speak with the dead - to be entirely plausible, if not demonstrably true.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: The Milesians - our ancestors, at least for those Irish in the room - did not start their story in Ireland, but were a group of people who had travelled the Earth for many hundreds of years.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: They came from Iberia, first led by a man named Íth, who met with the three high kings of Ireland - members of the Tuatha Dé Danann.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: He also met his end in Ireland, though the myths do not agree as to who or what killed him.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: Regardless, descendants of his brother’s line - the three brothers Amergin, Éremon, and Éber Finn - would later come to Ireland, seeking vengeance for Íth’s death.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: To do so, their forces travelled to the royal capital of Ireland to confront the kings he held responsible for their uncle’s demise.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: Along the way, his party met three goddesses - Banba, Fódhla, and Ériu -the wives of the three high kings, all of them both goddesses and embodiments of the land - a motif we discussed earlier.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: Each of them promised that they would bring them good luck, if they would only name the land after them.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: The Milesians and the high kings negotiated a truce, in which the Milesians would stay three days anchored offshore in their fleet -

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: But it was a trick! The Tuatha Dé Danann conjured a storm to wreck their foe's fleet.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: However, Amergin was a legendary poet, and calmed the winds with magical verse.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: Those ships that outlasted the storms took again to land, and - after great wars were waged - the survivors negotiated their peace.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: When offered half of the land, the Milesians agreed - and cunningly took the upper half, relegating the Tuatha Dé Danann to the Otherworld below.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: The land above was divided by Amergin between his brothers, giving the north to Éremon and the south to Éber Finn.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: They became the new high kings of Ireland - then known in the Irish tongue as Éire, in tribute to one of the sovereignty goddesses of old.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: I hope this gives you an understanding of where we've come from. Of the kinds of people we are.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: It concerns the most ancient reaches of our mythology, a time when a godlike race, the Tuatha De Danann...

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: ... also known as the Aos Sí or the Fair Folk - as my aunt has already spoken of to you - were the primary inhabitants of the land.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: Indeed, many is the god that has died at human hands. Or close enough to how we see death for it to be functionally the same in our eyes.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: They became the new high kings of Ireland - named under their rule, in the Irish tongue, Éire, after one of the goddesses that had so decreed it.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: I hope you might better understand this place now; that you might appreciate it more keenly, whether you are of this land or not.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: A people who cannot be wiped out, who can overcome any force and the tricks they may use.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: A people who will not stop until this land is theirs once more.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: If I have not yet had the pleasure of making your acquaintance, then please let me introduce myself.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: My name is Lloyd Dupré, and I am honoured to have this opportunity to speak with you all.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: My topic today will be the gods of Ireland, how gods can be adopted and changed by their uptake across the world...

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: And what it is that inspires the continued worship of a god, even when they may no longer be in their original context and form.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Detective Ward
en: [ STAY AND LISTEN ]

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Detective Ward
en: [ LEAVE ]

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Ward
en: Excuse me.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: First of all, we’ll discuss the gods native to Ireland, worshipped before the adoption of Christianity in the region.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: I’m afraid we won’t have time to talk about them all, as there are many, and many of them have quite extensive myths…

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: But we will talk about some of the foremost among them.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: The Mórrigan is a goddess in three parts, sometimes referred to as a singular woman, sometimes as three sisters...

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: Or sometimes as a singular goddess with three distinct aspects.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: No matter which form she is thought to take, she is a fearsome goddess; one thought to hold the domains of battle, and thusly victory and doom.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: She is a guardian of the battlefield, inspiring bravery in warriors and terror in their enemies.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: And perhaps due to her close link to death through battle, she is often associated with the crow - even appearing as one in certain myths.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: Lesser known, perhaps because she seems more unique to the more northern European experience, is the Cailleach.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: She is recognised across the British Isles - not as an exact copy, of course - but with recognisable similarities.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: She is understood to be a “hag”, a goddess in the form of an older woman to symbolise wisdom.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: And she is another fearsome goddess at that, well respected, but considered to have power over storms and winter... so not one you want to displease.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: There are other gods, too, with domains less directly tied to the natural world and instead to society.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: Goibniu, the smith god, was a much respected figure and, with a secondary domain of hospitality, was intrinsically tied to societal aspects of life.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: The goddess Brigid, beside him also had some domain over smithcraft, though her associations were more widely spread.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: She was thought to be a goddess of smithing, but also of poetry and healing - each attributed to one of the "sisters".

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: It is Brigid I wish to focus on, for now, as she provides a wonderful example of how mythology and religion may be adopted across the world.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: Like the goddess Mórrigan, she was sometimes said to have two sisters, though this may also be interpreted as her having a three-fold, or “triplicate” form.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: Where I am from, the city of New Orleans in the state of Louisiana, itself in the United States of America, there can be seen a unique mythology and religion.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: North America is a primarily Christian country.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: However, as I’m sure you’re aware, before the Abolitionary Act of 1865, a great many people were displaced from their homes by slavers.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: These people brought with them their cultures, and the gods and the worship they were accustomed to.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: One of these figures of worship was the Loa, the spirit, Maman Brigitte. Does the name sound familiar?

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: The truth is, that as they were unable to worship openly, practitioners of voodoo took to worshipping Saints found in the Catholic tradition, the Saints being guises for their Loas.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: This is a practice called syncretism, combining schools of religious thought.  Maman Brigitte is worshipped, if not as herself, occasionally as Mary Magdalene…

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: But more often, as Saint Brigid of Kildare, the Christian interpretation of the goddess Brigid, for their shared association with fire and snakes.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: It is my opinion that characters of gods hold particular sway across the world if they have a domain that is common to the human experience.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: And while we no longer live in an age of warriors and great battles, such as that the Mórrigan was said to oversee…

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: Now, Maman Brigitte is the guardian of cemeteries and the dead, and she protects those who have been laid to rest...

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: Bríd, goddess of poets, would surely still have domain with the authors of our age...

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: And one must imagine the spirit of Giobniu would be found in the Industrial Revolution that makes so much possible.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: The domains of gods are not lost, not to those that would worship them. They simply change.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: Across time and continents, their domains still hold meaning even if they take forms we no longer recognise. Such is the nature of things.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: Dear guests, I would like to thank each and every one of you for attending.

conversation: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: Feel free to chat with me later if you have any further questions.

Whatever the reason, we must free it! 
And I know how...

conversation: First floor/Sinnott's room/sigil reveal in room

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop D'Arcy and Dupré
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: And there are pockets of Irish people there, too.

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop D'Arcy and Dupré
speaker: Missus D'Arcy
en: Is that how you ended up here?

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop D'Arcy and Dupré
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: ...It is.

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop D'Arcy and Dupré
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: I have... had a friend.

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop D'Arcy and Dupré
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: She died. Not long ago. On her deathbed, she made me promise I'd bury her on her home soil. And so I am here.

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop D'Arcy and Dupré
speaker: Missus D'Arcy
en: And is she from around here? Is that how you ended up at the manor?

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop D'Arcy and Dupré
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: No, she's from the east - Louth. And no, I came here on the hope that the claims were real - that Miss Mantovani could let us actually speak with the dead.

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop D'Arcy and Dupré
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: I could feel her presence with me on the voyage here. I suspect her spirit resided with her ashes.

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop D'Arcy and Dupré
speaker: Missus D'Arcy
en: Resided? Have you lain her to rest, then?

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop D'Arcy and Dupré
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: No, her ashes are in my room. But since coming here, I...

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop D'Arcy and Dupré
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: ...it doesn't matter. I don't want to dwell on it with such good company.

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop D'Arcy and Dupré

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop D'Arcy and Dupré

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop D'Arcy and Dupré

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop D'Arcy and Dupré

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop, Skerritt and Coventry

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop, Skerritt and Coventry
speaker: Mister Coventry
en: No, I confess, I'm a novice to the whole thing.

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop, Skerritt and Coventry
speaker: Mister Coventry
en: But this séance sounded so fascinating! When I heard of it, I couldn't bring myself not to come along.

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop, Skerritt and Coventry
speaker: Mister Skerritt
en: No one could fault you for your lack of ambition.

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop, Skerritt and Coventry
speaker: Mister Coventry
en: Ambition? If you like! Mere curiosity, really.

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop, Skerritt and Coventry
speaker: Mister Coventry
en: Who isn't a little interested in whatever comes next? Especially at our age!

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop, Skerritt and Coventry
speaker: Mister Skerritt
en: Well, quite.

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop, Coventry, Ivy and Lan Fen
speaker: Mister Coventry
en: So, if I might ask - do you ladies find yourselves at events like this often?

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop, Coventry, Ivy and Lan Fen
speaker: Miss McLeod
en: Quite often - I've attended more than my fair share. Mostly in London, but not always.

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop, Coventry, Ivy and Lan Fen
speaker: Miss McLeod
en: But an entire week, with the ultimate goal of some grand ritual... Nothing like this has ever been done before!

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop, Coventry, Ivy and Lan Fen
speaker: Missus Lau
en: It seems more the venture of one of the secret societies than that of a seer.

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop, Coventry, Ivy and Lan Fen
speaker: Miss McLeod
en: That's true. I think that is why we found it so enticing!

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop, Coventry, Ivy and Lan Fen
speaker: Mister Coventry
en: Then you're not of a society yourselves?

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop, Coventry, Ivy and Lan Fen
speaker: Miss McLeod
en: No. I have a... gift, and I enjoy the company of those who would believe it. And Victoria, in her infinite patience, is here at my behest.

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop, Coventry, Ivy and Lan Fen
speaker: Missus Lau
en: It's not patience. After all, this has been a more interesting week than I would be having otherwise.

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Varley finds you at window

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Varley finds you at window

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Varley finds you at window

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Varley finds you at window

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop, dupre and O Finn

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop, dupre and O Finn
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: I learned a great deal from her.

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop, dupre and O Finn
speaker: Mister Ó Finn
en: Ah, so that's why you're here.

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop, dupre and O Finn
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: Yes. I've come to scatter her ashes in her homeland. It was her last request.

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop, dupre and O Finn
speaker: Mister Ó Finn
en: Aye. You can travel all you like, but the heart never leaves home. Not really.

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop, dupre and O Finn
speaker: Mister Ó Finn
en: Where will you put her?

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop, dupre and O Finn
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: I'm... not sure what to do with her. Not yet.

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop, dupre and O Finn
speaker: Mister Ó Finn
en: Well, if it's Bríd she looked to, you could do worse than to take her to Faughart, up by Dundalk in Louth.

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop, dupre and O Finn
speaker: Mister Ó Finn
en: Not a bad place to spend eternity.

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop, dupre and O Finn
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: That sounds nice. Thank you, Mister Ó Finn.

conversation: Outside/walled garden/Conversations/Eavesdrop, dupre and O Finn

conversation: Outside/Graveyard/conversations/arwa and cathal
speaker: Miss Hisham
en: ...over a hundred years ago, a vase was unearthed from an unidentified tomb in what used to be Nubia. It was found with the canopic jars.

conversation: Outside/Graveyard/conversations/arwa and cathal
speaker: Mister O'Meara
en: Rotted away?

conversation: Outside/Graveyard/conversations/arwa and cathal
speaker: Miss Hisham
en: No. There are mummified hearts that have lasted thousands of years. And the jar was still sealed.

conversation: Outside/Graveyard/conversations/arwa and cathal
speaker: Miss Hisham
en: The distinction is, to be particular, that archaeologists study physical objects. But much of it is found buried, yes.

conversation: Outside/Graveyard/conversations/arwa and cathal
speaker: Mister O'Meara
en: And that is where you found those jars for me?

conversation: Outside/Graveyard/conversations/arwa and cathal
speaker: Miss Hisham
en: It took the place, among the set, of the jar that would have held the entombed's heart - and yet, it was empty.

conversation: Outside/Graveyard/conversations/arwa and cathal
speaker: Mister O'Meara
en: And whose tomb was it?

conversation: Outside/Graveyard/conversations/arwa and cathal
speaker: Miss Hisham
en: It was unmarked. Unknown.

conversation: Outside/Graveyard/conversations/arwa and cathal
speaker: Miss Hisham
en: Likely, whoever was buried there wished to be unknown... or forgotten.

conversation: Outside/Graveyard/conversations/arwa and cathal
speaker: Miss Hisham
en: In short, yes. But I was on the hunt for something else - a vase.

conversation: Outside/Graveyard/conversations/arwa and cathal
speaker: Miss Hisham
en: I think it was the real final resting place of Nectanebo II.

conversation: Outside/Graveyard/conversations/arwa and cathal
speaker: Mister O'Meara
en: Oh?

conversation: Outside/Graveyard/conversations/arwa and cathal
speaker: Miss Hisham
en: His royal sarcophagus was never used. He fled after defeat by the Persians and ended up in...

conversation: Outside/Graveyard/conversations/arwa and cathal
speaker: Miss Hisham
en: Yes, exactly this. Notably, he was considered to be a powerful magician.

conversation: Outside/Graveyard/conversations/arwa and cathal
speaker: Mister O'Meara
en: So you suspect the missing heart is related to that?

conversation: Outside/Graveyard/conversations/arwa and cathal
speaker: Miss Hisham
en: I do not think the heart was missing. I think... perhaps it was destroyed in some ritual of his?

conversation: Outside/Graveyard/conversations/arwa and cathal
speaker: Miss Hisham
en: Thanks to our Miss Deane, I now know the last documented person to have had the vase - Barnard Blake. A great-granduncle of the Marquess, though he never held the title himself.

conversation: Outside/Graveyard/conversations/arwa and cathal
speaker: Mister O'Meara
en: And you think your vase... it is here?

conversation: Outside/Graveyard/conversations/arwa and cathal
speaker: Miss Hisham

conversation: Outside/Graveyard/conversations/arwa and cathal
speaker: Mister O'Meara
en: Well, good luck to you. If I can help, I will. I am indebted for the jars.

conversation: Outside/Graveyard/conversations/arwa and cathal
speaker: Miss Hisham

conversation: Outside/Graveyard/conversations/arwa and cathal

conversation: Outside/Graveyard/conversations/arwa and cathal

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Comments from Ward/Post-Ritual Cutscene

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Comments from Ward/Post-Ritual Cutscene
speaker: Missus Joyce
en: I'll not suffer to think about it, Sir.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Comments from Ward/Post-Ritual Cutscene
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: Thank you, Missus Joyce. That would be much appreciated.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Comments from Ward/Post-Ritual Cutscene
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: Th-thank you, Mister Ward. Both of you.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Comments from Ward/Post-Ritual Cutscene
speaker: Mister Dupré

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Comments from Ward/Post-Ritual Cutscene
speaker: Missus Joyce

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Comments from Ward/Post-Ritual Cutscene
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: I know what you mean. It's as if some part of it felt it to be unsafe. But now? I think Laura is watching over us and wants us to be there.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Comments from Ward/Post-Ritual Cutscene
speaker: Missus Joyce
en: Come. Let's get you inside - I'll make you a hot cup of tea.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Comments from Ward/Paper reveal

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Comments from Ward/Paper reveal

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Comments from Ward/Paper read
speaker: Mister Ward
en: Did someone try to burn this?

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Comments from Ward/Paper read
speaker: Mister Ward
en: Either way, whatever survived is readable...

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Comments from Ward/Paper read
speaker: Mister Ward

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Comments from Ward/Paper read
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "Evelyn Deane WILL be the vessel. She must contain Laura's spirit, the universe begs for it by her design."

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Comments from Ward/Paper read
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "She will return to me. here. HERE. NO. One, two, three, Maman save me from darkness, one, two, three,"

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Comments from Ward/Paper read
speaker: Mister Ward

speaker: Mister Ward
en: "burn it burn it bu-"

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Comments from Ward/Paper read
speaker: Mister Ward
en: ...Sweet lord.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Comments from Ward/Paper read
speaker: Mister Ward
en: "evelyn evelyn evelyn maman evelynevelyn Evelyn. Deane."

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Comments from Ward/Paper read
speaker: Mister Ward

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Comments from Ward/Paper read
speaker: Mister Ward

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Comments from Ward/Paper read
speaker: Mister Ward

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Darragh and Ivy conversation
speaker: Mister Hunter
en: What excuse would you have to come to a place like this, lass?

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Darragh and Ivy conversation
speaker: Miss McLeod
en: If I had known you were here, I would have made my excuses much earlier. You could have told me!

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Darragh and Ivy conversation
speaker: Miss McLeod
en: A fervent desire for - more rain?

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Darragh and Ivy conversation
speaker: Mister Hunter
en: Hah! That might've done it. But I thought maybe it would be best to let you get along with things. And you've done well at it, it seems.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Darragh and Ivy conversation
speaker: Mister Hunter
en: Not that I haven't missed you. It's good to see you. How're things back home, as it goes?

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Darragh and Ivy conversation
speaker: Miss McLeod
en: Oh, well - Johnny got married last Spring. And mother's got plans for Cecil, though he's doing what he does best, and avoiding that at all costs...

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Darragh and Ivy conversation
speaker: Miss McLeod
en: He will come around to it. But he's usually in Edinburgh, not home. So these days, when I am home, it's only me and mother and father.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Darragh and Ivy conversation
speaker: Miss McLeod
en: We have a new stable master, of course, but I don't like him half as much as you. Neither do the boys, I don't think.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Darragh and Ivy conversation
speaker: Mister Hunter
en: I would be hurt if you did, love. But... how are you these days, with the an da shealladh?

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Darragh and Ivy conversation
speaker: Miss McLeod
en: I do alright, I think... but they still don't know what to do with me. That's why I spend all that time in London these days.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Darragh and Ivy conversation
speaker: Miss McLeod
en: They don't know of the tradition like people back home... but at least there are all these people that like to hear about it.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Darragh and Ivy conversation
speaker: Mister Hunter
en: It's quite the collection, if the people attending this thing are anything to go by. Speaking of the like...

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Darragh and Ivy conversation
speaker: Mister Hunter
en: How are you, lass, with your Sight?

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Darragh and Ivy conversation
speaker: Miss McLeod
en: I wish I could say. It's still... it's not back. And if it is, it's too... blurry to see. Hard to think I would miss it, but it doesn't feel right not to have it either.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Darragh and Ivy conversation
speaker: Mister Hunter
en: All being as it should be, it'll be better soon.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Dupré
speaker: Miss Callaghan
en: There will not be any sound, mind you. It's more like looking through a mirror.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Dupré
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: Of course, I understand. I don't mind that. It will be good just to see them.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Dupré
speaker: Miss Callaghan
en: You have to concentrate. Let your mind go quiet, and focus on who you want to see.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Dupré
speaker: Miss Callaghan
en: ...Yes, exactly like that.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Dupré
speaker: Miss Callaghan
en: Who is that, your mother?

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Dupré
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: My aunt, and my nephew beside her.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Dupré
speaker: Miss Callaghan
en: They look well. And they're all the way in Louisiana?

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Dupré
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: They are. The journey is a long one. It's been a while since I've seen them, and a while more until I can see them again.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Dupré
speaker: Miss Callaghan
en: Of course. It's such a long way. I don't envy you, being so far from home.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Dupré
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: It is different here, and a little lonely, but it's not without good company.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Dupré
speaker: Miss Callaghan
en: If you focus well enough. Give it a try.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Dupré
speaker: Miss Callaghan
en: Oh, look at that! You're a natural.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Dupré
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: If I think of someone else, will we see them?

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Saoirse
speaker: Miss Callaghan
en: There you are.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Saoirse
speaker: Miss Callaghan
en: Come here, now. Have you done this before, a leanbh?

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Saoirse
speaker: Miss Murphy
en: No, Miss. I've never... I didn't know it would really work. ...Does it?

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Saoirse
speaker: Miss Callaghan
en: It most certainly does. Come here, and stand beside me.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Saoirse
speaker: Miss Callaghan
en: You'll want to look into the well, and try and get your thoughts calm. Take all the time you need.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Saoirse
speaker: Miss Murphy

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Saoirse
speaker: Miss Callaghan
en: Deep breaths, there. Now I want you to think about your daughter. Do your best to picture her in your mind.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Saoirse
speaker: Miss Callaghan
en: Look at that; there you go.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Saoirse
speaker: Miss Murphy
en: That's her?

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Saoirse
speaker: Miss Callaghan
en: She has your eyes, does she not?

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Saoirse
speaker: Miss Murphy
en: She looks alright. She looks... she looks well. I was so worried, I...

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Saoirse
speaker: Miss Callaghan

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Saoirse
speaker: Miss Callaghan
en: I hope you'll get to see her again someday. But until then... I can show you how to do this for yourself, too, you know?

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Saoirse
speaker: Miss Murphy
en: You... Really?

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Saoirse
speaker: Miss Callaghan
en: It's no trouble at all, sweetheart.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Saoirse
speaker: Miss Murphy
en: I've no words, that'd be... Thank you. So, so much.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Carmela
speaker: Miss Mantovani

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Carmela

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Carmela
speaker: Miss Mantovani

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Carmela
speaker: Miss Callaghan

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Carmela
speaker: Miss Mantovani
en: My family, of course!

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Carmela
speaker: Miss Mantovani
en: Except… No. When I think of them, I imagine what these people would say of me... Leaving them as I did...

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Carmela
speaker: Miss Callaghan
en: …You put too much on yourself.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Carmela
speaker: Miss Mantovani
en: Hah! Santo cielo - says she, carrier of woes.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Carmela
speaker: Miss Callaghan
en: Well, I’d rather carry woes than expectations.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Carmela
speaker: Miss Callaghan
en: Sometimes we just need to put down the load, Carmela.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Carmela
speaker: Miss Mantovani
en: Oh, I see them. Ah, but I forgot how good it feels to see them. It has been so long, and I am so far from home...

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Carmela
speaker: Miss Mantovani
en: Ah, cielo. Is that rain?

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Carmela
speaker: Miss Mantovani
en: …Oh.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Carmela
speaker: Miss Mantovani
en: But what choice did I have? A magician must glitter! Whatever mud she is born in, she must bloom and escape to survive!

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Carmela
speaker: Miss Callaghan
en: The mind must be relaxed, but focused. Not so easy, at least not at first.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Corentine
speaker: Miss Callaghan
en: She seems a sweet girl. How old is she?

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Corentine

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Corentine

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Corentine
speaker: Miss Quinn
en: I only said she'll be fourteen.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Corentine
speaker: Miss Callaghan

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Corentine
speaker: Miss Quinn
en: It so happens I might be the closest Alma has, these days.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Corentine
speaker: Miss Callaghan
en: That's a terrible burden for someone so young.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Corentine
speaker: Miss Quinn
en: No. It's a privilege. I hope I get to continue it.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Corentine
speaker: Miss Quinn

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh and Ruairi after minigame

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh and Ruairi after minigame

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh and Ruairi after minigame

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh and Ruairi after minigame

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh and Ruairi after minigame
speaker: Miss Callaghan
en: I'm... sorry Ruairí.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh and Ruairi after minigame
speaker: Miss Callaghan
en: I've been too hard on your ways. Too hard on you.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh and Ruairi after minigame
speaker: Miss Callaghan
en: I wanted the old way to be the only way. Maybe because I am the old way.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh and Ruairi after minigame
speaker: Miss Callaghan
en: Maybe I'm not ready to hand over the role yet...

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh and Ruairi after minigame
speaker: Miss Callaghan
en: ...but now I know that when I do, you're ready for it.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh and Ruairi after minigame
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: Thank you, Fiadh. That means a lot.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh and Ruairi after minigame
speaker: Doctor Callaghan
en: Now. What was that green glow?

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh and Ruairi after minigame

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh and Ruairi after minigame

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh and Ruairi after minigame

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Carmela and Dupré, Carmela's health

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Carmela and Dupré, Carmela's health

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Carmela and Dupré, Carmela's health
speaker: Miss Mantovani

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Carmela and Dupré, Carmela's health
speaker: Miss Mantovani
en: I will make the best of it, I think.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Carmela and Dupré, Carmela's health
speaker: Mister Dupré
en: ...Can I do anything for you?

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Carmela and Dupré, Carmela's health
speaker: Miss Mantovani
en: ...You stay here with me for a moment? I do not want to be alone just now.

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Carmela and Dupré, Carmela's health
speaker: Miss Mantovani

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Carmela and Dupré, Carmela's health

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Saoirse Post Quest

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Saoirse after seeing kiddo

conversation: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Saoirse after seeing kiddo

conversation: Document Texts/Hiring Telegram
speaker: Varley
en:
Mister Ward, October 27th
I'll waste no time, as there's none for wasting. I write from Blake Manor in Connemara. Yesterday, a guest went missing - a young woman named Evelyn Deane (photograph enclosed). Everyone here carries on as if nothing has happened but her room's not been slept in nor have any locals seen her off hotel grounds - she has not left, of that I am sure.
This envelope contains two-hundred pounds. Please, Sir, accept this money and come quick. I fear she's not long for this world. A further three-hundred pounds will be paid out if you find her alive.
I know the West of Ireland might well be the far side of the world for its distance from you, but there's no one else to turn to. I hear you are an honourable man, a steadfast investigator, and - perhaps most importantly - godly.
I pray for the girl that this is true. Sincerely, A concerned party.

conversation: Document Texts/Letter from Doctor Callaghan
speaker: Varley
en:
Miss Deane,
I hope you'll forgive me the delay in reaching out to you - there has been an influx of influenza patients in Dublin, and the hospital has a great many of us working all hours.
I know my aunt has rejected your request for training in our magic, but she is overly concerned with tradition and lineages and things being done the way they have always been. I am less held by the old ways and its restrictions. Indeed, I think new paths and partnerships are required to keep the traditions alive.
I'll be attending the Grand Séance in Blake Manor, unexpected flu season or not. Let us meet there and discuss what you want to learn?
For my part, I do not ask payment for this. Instead, a favour - I intend to make inroads to the London scene and the right contacts would make it easier. Contacts I know you have.
What say you, Miss Deane? A trade?
Doctor Ruairí Callaghan.

conversation: Document Texts/Letter from Doctor Callaghan
speaker: Varley
en:
Miss Deane, I hope you'll forgive me the delay in responding to your letter - there has been an influx of influenza patients in Dublin, and the hospital has a great many of us working all hours. I was rather looking forward to some time back in Connacht, but it seems that won't be on the cards for some time - so for now I remain in Dublin. I'll undoubtedly be attending this Grand Séance, unexpected flu season or not. I don't see how I could do anything else. With it so close to home, missing it is inconceivable. You are, of course, welcome to visit if you decide you wish to make more of a holiday out of your time in the county. Regarding the reception the event is getting, from what I've heard it is largely welcomed. There is some talk, as there often is, of the idea being rather too close to farming out our traditions - but it seems a hysterical opinion in this case, when séances are not in the slightest distinctly Irish. I don't disagree it could, hypothetically, become a concern, but in this case I find it baseless. The same people ought to consider, as you have said yourself, that they're very fond of Egyptian practices, these and European practices frequently being brought to London and so to Dublin. Frankly, there ought to be made some sort of consensus. Some sort of middle ground of adoption and conservation - or any sort of learned practice in these circles will become the domain of hypocrites alone. If you ask me, I think the greatest concern for all involved is not what I've outlined above, but the practising of borrowed magic without due consideration. I know you to be a sensible woman, of course, but I would worry about any peer in that Order of yours that does not properly consider the powers they wish to invoke. Or, for that matter, anyone outside of it whose interest is caught. There are those that underestimate the matters we deal with, as you well know. There is a great deal of nuance I would go on to outline, had I the time. In lieu, I hope we can discuss this when we meet for this Grand Séance instead. It will be a sincere pleasure to see you again. Yours faithfully,
Doctor Ruairí Callaghan.

conversation: Document Texts/Missing Pages From Miss Deane's Journal
speaker: Varley
en:
Corentine is attending the Grand Séance. I should have expected to see her here, of course, but she had kept such a low profile after our... disagreement.
I do regret it, of course. I should have been a more loyal friend but I had to view that book while I could. I would say that the cost to entry was too high, but I would pay it again. And again.
I didn't think she cared so much for standing. I thought she'd understand but my betrayal has clearly done more harm than anticipated. She barely acknowledged me and when I called her name, she looked at me with such anger in her eyes...
I may try again to mend things between us but she's in her books like never before. I doubt I will get near her.

conversation: Document Texts/Missing Pages From Miss Deane's Journal
speaker: Varley
en:
Corentine is attending the Grand Séance. I didn't expect to see her here. She nodded to me when she saw me, addressed me by my name, and then didn't say much at all else to me. She's in her books like never before.
I had the mind to make amends such as I could, but either she's twice as stubborn as she's ever been, or I did her more harm than I knew. It was not a pretty situation at all, but she was very clear she wants nothing more to do with me.
It's a shame. I should have liked to talk to her about this event. I'd say I miss her, but I don't want to start thinking like that, or I'll make myself sad before this event even gets going. Maybe there's nothing for it all after all, except perhaps time.

conversation: Document Texts/Mister D'Arcy's letters
speaker: Varley
en:
There are several letters, among them one dated from late August 1896 that seems to have been read several times over.
...and when I go to these things, I can't help but think that I'd like them so much more if only you'd accompany me, Cecil. Rosemary would have been the most awful play I'd ever attended if it hadn't been with you. You have a way of making the most mundane things so intriguing, so new and curiously handsome, as if under a new light entirely. You make me feel the same way, you know, when you hold me - as if I am made anew and entirely more interesting. And I know, too, that I very interesting indeed to you.
And so - for the sake of interest - do make your excuses and join me at a so-called Grand Séance in Ireland next year. Just how grand it will be remains to be seen, of course, but I think it has promise. And if it is dull, we shall just have to make our own entertainment.

conversation: Document Texts/Ivy's journal entry (about Deane)
speaker: Varley
en:
October 27th.
Just my luck, that Evelyn Deane is attending this séance too. Is it too much to ask that I manage to find one such event where she is not plying her trade? Whatever that trade may be - what it is at the moment, I truly don't know. I fear if she takes to claiming to have a gift for visions, she'll become favoured for it, and I will become so obscure as to be overlooked. And what then? Visions of death and tragedy and no one to listen to them? Another ten years of suffering them quietly? I shall go mad entirely.

conversation: Document Texts/Ines' journal entry
speaker: Varley
en: It's been two months since the funeral. Still, I turn to speak with my mother when a thought occurs to me. No one answers, of course. There's no one there to. I always knew there'd be a day like this, and yet I was not prepared. I am in the middle of it all, and still not prepared. I'm stuck trying to speak to people that aren't there anymore, or never were.

speaker: Varley

Apprentice Skerritt,
We have been back and forth on this. You have been in the order for many years, and yet you have not grasped its core tenets.
Your obsession with advancement has blinded you to the very ways to advance! Progress is gained through fraternity, charity, and self-sacrifice.
The fact that, despite many requests to stop doing so, you continue to wear your father's badge and claim his rank to impress people just shows how little you respect the order, its rites, and its processes.
Whatever secrets you seek are not for sale. They must be earned. Since you are unwilling to work towards them, it has been decided to evict you from the lodge.
We wish you well, Mister Skerritt, but do not return here. Then, across the letter, the following note is scrawled: "They deny me their magic! What kind of legacy can I forge by mundane means alone!?"
